*** {{audio|en|en-us-mate.ogg|a=US}}
** {{IPA|en|[mɛjt]|a=SSB}}
** {{IPA|en|[meːt]|a=CA,Scotland}}
** {{IPA|en|[mæɪt]|a=AU}}
*** {{audio|en|en-au-mate.ogg|a=AU}}
* {{rhymes|en|eɪt|s=1}}

===Etymology 1===
{{root|en|ine-pro|*meh₂d- (wet)}}
{{etymon|en|id=partner|:inh|enm:mate<id:noun>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|mate}}, borrowed from {{der|en|gml|mate||messmate}}, earlier {{m|gml|gemate}}, with loss of the prefix. From {{der|en|osx|*gimato}}, from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*gamatō}},<ref name="KlugeBasis">{{cite-book|de|author=Friedrich Kluge|year=1911|title=Seemannssprache|pages=561–562|url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Seemannsprache/BygnAAAAMAAJ}}</ref> from {{der|en|gem-pro|*gamatô||messmate, table companion}}.<ref name="OED2mate">{{R:OED2|mate|volume=IX}} Etymology reproduced in the [https://uitleenwoordenbank.ivdnt.org/index.php/uitleen/zoek_gecombineerd_cached?initiaal=M&sort=alf Uitleenwoordenbank].</ref>

Compare native {{cog|enm|mett}}, {{m|enm|mette||table companion, mate, partner}}, from {{cog|ang|ġemetta||sharer of food, table‐guest}}, which reflects the related {{m|gem-pro|*gamatjô}}.<ref name="OED2mate"/>

Related terms include {{cog|nds-de|Maat||journeyman, companion}}, {{cog|de|Maat||naval non‐commissioned officer}}, {{cog|nl|maat||mate, partner, colleague, friend}} and {{cog|stq|Moat||friend, buddy, comrade, mate}}. More at {{cog|ang|ġe-}}, {{cog|en|co-}}, {{cog|en|meat}}. {{doublet|en|maat}}.

Compare typologically {{m+|la|compāniō}} (whence {{m|en|companion}}) (< {{m|la|con-}} + {{m|la|panis}} + {{m|la|-ō}}), {{m+|ru|однока́шник}} (< {{m|ru|одно-}} + {{m|ru|ка́ша}} + {{m|ru|-ник}}).

Probably originally a seamen's term, as English, Dutch and German borrowed the word from the same Middle Low German source.<ref name="EWN">M. Philippa et al., ''Etymologisch Woordenboek van het Nederlands'', Amsterdam 2003–2009, s.v. ''maat 2'' ([https://etymologiebank.nl/trefwoord/maat2 etymologiebank.nl]).</ref>

====Noun====
{{en-noun}}

# A [[fellow]], [[comrade]], [[colleague]], [[partner]] or someone with whom something is shared, e.g. shipmate, classmate.
#: {{syn|en|fellow|fere|q2=poetic, archaic}}
# {{lb|en|especially of a non-human [[animal]]}} A [[breed]]ing partner.
#* {{RQ:Guardian|date=2015-04-16|author=w:Richard P. Grant|title=Sex and the successful fundraiser|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/occams-corner/2015/apr/16/sex-and-the-successful-fundraiser|passage=Such overt displays of avowed sexual prowess – or at least, desperate availability – are not limited to the countryside. Even in the city, birds and animals and stockbrokers and nurses find ways of signalling their suitability as a '''mate'''.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20261013060742/https://www.theguardian.com/science/occams-corner/2015/apr/16/sex-and-the-successful-fundraiser|archivedate=13 October 2026}}
# {{lb|en|colloquial|British|Australia|New Zealand|Ireland|South Africa|sometimes elsewhere in the Commonwealth}} A [[friend]], usually of the same sex.
#: {{syn|en|friend|buddy|Thesaurus:friend}}
#: {{ux|en|I'm going to the pub with a few '''mates'''.}}
#: {{ux|en|He's my best '''mate'''.}}
# {{lb|en|colloquial|British|Australia|New Zealand|Ireland|South Africa|sometimes elsewhere in the Commonwealth}} Friendly term of address to a stranger, usually male, of similar age.
#: {{syn|en|buddy}}
#: {{ux|en|Excuse me, '''mate''', have you got the time?}}
# {{lb|en|nautical}} In [[naval]] ranks, a [[non-commissioned officer]] or his subordinate (e.g. {{w|Boatswain's Mate}}, {{w|Gunner's Mate}}, Sailmaker's Mate, etc).
# {{lb|en|nautical}} A [[ship]]'s [[officer]], [[subordinate]] to the [[master]] on a commercial ship.
# {{lb|en|nautical}} A [[first mate]].
# A [[technical]] [[assistant]] in certain trades (e.g. ''gasfitter's mate'', ''plumber's mate''); sometimes an [[apprentice]].
# The other [[member]] of a [[match]]ed [[pair]] of objects.
#: {{ux|en|I found one of the socks I wanted to wear, but I couldn't find its '''mate'''.}}
# A suitable companion; a match; an equal.
#* {{RQ:Milton Paradise Lost|book=IV|passage=Ye knew me once no '''mate''' / For you; there sitting where you durst not soar.|year=1873}}

=====Usage notes=====
{{rfref|en}}
* In British and Irish English, ''mate'' remains more masculine‐leaning, though it is increasingly used as a gender‐neutral term among younger generations and in urban centres. In Australian and New Zealand English, while it was originally strictly masculine, it has broadened in recent decades to become a common unisex term of address, even when speaking to strangers.
* The use of this term in the homosocial maritime and working‐class environments from the late 14th to the 19th century fostered a strong connotation of egalitarianism and male solidarity. In colonial Australia and New Zealand, the term also denoted an equal partner in a joint enterprise, especially on the goldfields (a role filled by {{m|en|partner}} in North American English). The shift toward a unisex application is a relatively modern sociolinguistic development.
* In North America, this colloquial sense is rarely used natively and is strongly associated with British or Australasian speech. Instead, North American English relies on terms such as {{m|en|buddy}}, {{m|en|pal}}, or {{m|en|dude}}. In the US and Canada, ''mate'' is generally restricted to its biological sense (a breeding partner) or its formal nautical sense (as in ''first mate'').

We call them the first men—we speak their language quite as much as we do our own; only in the rituals of the temple do we make any attempt to retain our mother tongue. In time it will be forgotten, and we will speak only the language of the apes; in time we will no longer banish those of our people who '''mate''' with apes, and so in time we shall descend to the very beasts from which ages ago our progenitors may have sprung.”}}
